passage:
Week one, Monday. Ujjwal read the chapter on group consolidation for the third time and still couldn't see where the minority interest went. He shut the book at eleven and messaged his colleague Kishore: 'Is this meant to make sense?' Kishore sent back a laughing face and 'Eventually.'
Week five, Thursday. Same chapter, now with worked examples. He did two a night on the office printer's scrap paper, slowly, getting half of them wrong. It felt like walking in sand.
Week seven, Saturday. He was halfway through a new example when the whole thing turned over in his head at once: the parent, the subsidiary, the share nobody owned. It was obvious. He actually said 'oh' out loud in the empty flat.
He called Kishore. 'It clicked. Just now.'
'Just now?' Kishore said. 'Or after seven weeks?'

qa.q: On which day did the concept finally click for Ujjwal?
qa.a: It clicked on the Saturday of week seven.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when he said 'oh' out loud in the empty flat?
qa.a: He felt sudden surprise and delight, as if the understanding had arrived all at once.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal take from this breakthrough for the next hard chapter?
qa.a: He could trust the slow weeks of worked examples, because the 'sudden' click was built on them, and keep that steady routine.

qa.q: How does Kishore see Ujjwal's breakthrough?
qa.a: Kishore sees it as the result of seven weeks of quiet work, not a lucky moment, which is why Kishore teases 'Or after seven weeks?'

grounding: It shows a concept suddenly clicking after weeks, with the jump feeling sudden but resting on the slow consolidation of the plateau.

passage:
Akash, come, look at this sketch of yours. Wobbly? Mine were worse. When I was twenty-four, a girl fresh out of college, before these computers did it all, everyone called me 'little Jahnavi'. I worked in a small architect's office in Pune, and I could not draw a building in perspective to save my life. Two vanishing points, they told me. Simple. For five weeks my buildings leaned like they were drunk. I drew the same street corner every lunch break, on tracing paper, and binned most of it.
Then one evening, packing up, I tried the corner one more time and the lines just went where they should. The windows shrank properly. The pavement ran away from me. I sat there staring, almost scared to touch it in case it stopped working.
I thought it had happened that evening. It hadn't, Akash. Those five weeks of binned paper did it. That evening they just showed up.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi draw every lunch break for five weeks?
qa.a: She drew the same street corner every lunch break, on tracing paper.

qa.q: Why was Jahnavi almost scared to touch the drawing after it worked?
qa.a: She was so surprised by the sudden change that she half feared it was a fluke that might vanish.

qa.q: What choice did Jahnavi keep making during the five weeks her buildings leaned, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She kept drawing the same street corner every lunch break instead of giving up, and those binned sheets built the skill that finally showed up that evening.

qa.q: How did the people in the Pune office seem to see Jahnavi at first?
qa.a: They called her 'little Jahnavi' and thought two vanishing points were simple, so they seem to have seen her as a beginner still finding her feet.

grounding: It shows perspective drawing suddenly clicking after weeks, with the elder explaining that the breakthrough rested on the quiet consolidation before it.
